title: How Housing Discrimination Works
summary: Josh and Chuck examine housing discrimination in the United States and how it has built and blocked intergenerational wealth. They cover the racial wealth gap cited from a Brookings study, pre-industrial integration and the Great Migration-era segregation, New Deal agencies (HOLC and FHA) and their color-coded redlining maps, the exclusion of Black veterans from G.I. Bill mortgages, FHA-backed suburban construction and racial covenants, white flight and interstates through Black neighborhoods, gentrification and property tax burdens, blockbusting and racial steering by real estate agents, the appraisal undervaluation of Black-owned homes, subprime lending during the mortgage crisis, and paired testing studies showing ongoing discrimination. The episode ends with a lighter listener-mail segment about Necco wafers.

National Association of Real Estate Boards

segments.title: Opening and framing
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce the episode, thank scholars Dr. Villanueva Bashi Treitler and Tricia Rose for their help, and frame housing as a major source of intergenerational wealth in the United States.

segments.title: Wealth gap and early history of segregation
segments.summary: They cite a Brookings study on the median white and Black net worth gap and describe how segregation was less common before industrialization, then intensified with the Northern migration of Black Americans and white violence against them.

segments.title: HOLC and FHA redlining maps
segments.summary: The hosts explain how the New Deal's Home Owners Loan Corporation created color-coded grade maps from A to D, how the FHA produced similar maps, and how the red-lined areas, usually communities of color, were excluded from lending, giving rise to the term redlining.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Short break between segments with casual banter about nails and beer.

segments.title: Redlining effects and lending statistics
segments.summary: They discuss federally backed mortgage statistics from 1934 to 1962, the lasting homeownership gap, the effect of redlining on property values and neighborhood decline, and the study showing Black college graduates less likely to own homes than white high school dropouts.

segments.title: G.I. Bill and FHA suburbs
segments.summary: The hosts describe how the G.I. Bill's VA loans were used to discriminate against Black veterans, linking this to Southern Dixiecrat politics, and how FHA construction loans created postwar suburbs with racial covenants and restrictions against selling to Black buyers.

segments.title: White flight, interstates, and public housing
segments.summary: They discuss white flight from cities to suburbs, the resulting concentration of Black residents in cities, highways built through Black neighborhoods, underfunded public housing such as Pruitt-Igoe, and the myth that Black residents lower home values.

segments.title: Gentrification and property taxes
segments.summary: The hosts describe gentrification, rising taxes that push long-term lower-income residents out, a Neighbor in Need program that helps them, and Chuck's proposal to end property taxes after long residence.

segments.title: Blockbusting, steering, appraisal bias, and subprime loans
segments.summary: They cover blockbusting by real estate agents, the NAREB policy until 1950, racial steering documented by a 2006 National Fair Housing Alliance study, Brookings findings that Black-owned homes are undervalued by about $48,000, and disproportionate subprime lending during the mortgage crisis.

segments.title: Paired testing and current findings
segments.summary: The hosts explain paired testing developed by HUD in the 1970s and the Urban Institute findings that discrimination persists, with some decline since 1989, and that people with disabilities also face discrimination.

segments.title: Listener mail: Necco wafers
segments.summary: Instead of a specific letter, the hosts taste Necco wafers after listener feedback about them.
